consensus_summary: Wheat primarily symbolizes God’s faithful people—the righteous or true believers—who are gathered into the kingdom at the final judgment, especially in contrast with tares or chaff.
book_summary: Wheat is identified as the children of the kingdom, the good grain gathered into the barn at harvest, opposite the tares.
consensus_core_identification: The children of God’s kingdom or righteous believers.
boundary_disagreement: None material. The book states only the dominant judgment-parable sense and omits other context-dependent uses of wheat, but it does not deny or reclassify them.
material_contradiction: None. Both identify wheat in the cited harvest context with the children of the kingdom gathered by God.
rationale: The minimum core identifications are equivalent. The book’s language closely reproduces the consensus’s primary meaning and its contrast with tares, while its harvest-and-barn detail matches the same eschatological imagery. Omission of the consensus’s alternative meanings does not create an extension disagreement because the entry makes no claim that its identification governs every biblical occurrence of wheat.
strongest_objection: Matthew 13:38 literally identifies the good seed, rather than the mature wheat by name, as the children of the kingdom. Even so, the parable’s seed-to-crop continuity and Matthew 3:12’s explicit gathering of wheat strongly support the entry’s identification.
